lesson.title: The Speedometer Theorem: Introducing the Mean Value Theorem
lesson.summary: If you drive 120 miles in two hours, your average speed was 60 miles per hour, and the Mean Value Theorem guarantees that at some exact instant during the trip, your speedometer actually read 60. This section introduces that guarantee and the two conditions, continuity and differentiability, that make it work.
lesson.body:
Suppose you drive 120 miles in exactly 2 hours. Your average speed for the trip is 120/2 = 60 miles per hour. Common sense says that even though your speed surely varied, speeding up and slowing down along the way, there must have been at least one moment when your instantaneous speed, the actual speedometer reading, was exactly 60 miles per hour. You could not have driven the whole trip below 60 mph and still averaged 60, and you could not have driven the whole trip above 60 mph either; somewhere your instantaneous rate had to match the average rate. The Mean Value Theorem, often abbreviated MVT, is the precise, general statement of that everyday intuition, applied to any function describing continuous, smooth change, not just position over time.

The theorem needs two properties from the function on the interval in question, and each one earns its place. It needs the function to be continuous on the closed interval [a,b], meaning no breaks, jumps, or holes anywhere from a to b, including at the endpoints themselves; this connects directly to the idea of a continuous function. And it needs the function to be differentiable on the open interval (a,b), meaning it has a well defined tangent line, and hence an instantaneous rate of change, at every point strictly between a and b; this connects to the idea of a differentiable function. Continuity alone is not enough, because a continuous function can still have a sharp corner where no tangent line, and hence no instantaneous rate, exists. Differentiability on the open interval, not necessarily including the endpoints, turns out to be exactly the right amount of smoothness to guarantee the conclusion, no more and no less. Later sections build counterexamples showing what breaks when either condition is dropped.

Here is the guarantee in action on a simple function. Let f(x) = x^2 on the interval [0,2]. This is a polynomial, so it is continuous everywhere and differentiable everywhere, certainly satisfying both conditions on [0,2]. The average rate of change over the interval is [f(2) - f(0)] divided by (2 - 0), which is (4 - 0)/2 = 2. The Mean Value Theorem promises there is some c strictly between 0 and 2 where the instantaneous rate of change, f'(c), equals that average rate, 2. Since f'(x) = 2x, setting 2c = 2 gives c = 1, and indeed 1 lies in the open interval (0,2). Checking directly, f'(1) = 2(1) = 2, exactly the average rate. The theorem did not just promise a point c existed in the abstract; here it can actually be found.

The next few sections pin down the theorem's exact wording, dig into why each hypothesis is necessary, and explore what the conclusion means and how to use it, but the core idea is already visible in this example: for any function that changes continuously and smoothly enough over an interval, the average rate of change over the whole interval is always achieved as an actual instantaneous rate at some point inside it.
